title: March 2025 CPI: prices fall 0.1% on the month as gasoline drops; core rises 0.1%
summary: Seasonally adjusted consumer prices fell 0.1 percent in March after rising 0.2 percent in February, as gasoline fell 6.3 percent. Over 12 months prices rose 2.4 percent, down from 2.8 percent. Core prices rose 0.1 percent, and their 2.8 percent 12-month rise was the smallest since March 2021.

source.title: Consumer Price Index — March 2025
source.timezone_note: In April, Eastern Time is Eastern Daylight Time, UTC−04:00, so the release time is 12:30 UTC.

overview: The all items CPI-U fell 0.1 percent in March on a seasonally adjusted basis, after a 0.2 percent rise in February. Energy fell 2.4 percent as seasonally adjusted gasoline dropped 6.3 percent, more than offsetting increases in electricity and natural gas. Before seasonal adjustment gasoline fell only 0.9 percent, and the all items index itself rose 0.2 percent. Food rose 0.4 percent, with eggs up 5.9 percent.

Core prices rose 0.1 percent after 0.2 percent. Shelter rose 0.2 percent: owners' equivalent rent rose 0.4 percent and rent 0.3 percent, but lodging away from home fell 3.5 percent. Airline fares fell 5.3 percent after a 4.0 percent fall in February, and motor vehicle insurance, used cars and trucks, and recreation also fell. Core goods (commodities less food and energy commodities) fell 0.1 percent.

Over 12 months, all items rose 2.4 percent, down from 2.8 percent to February. Core rose 2.8 percent, the smallest 12-month increase since March 2021, and shelter 4.0 percent, the smallest since November 2021. Energy was down 3.3 percent over the year and food up 3.0 percent.

key_facts.label: Core, 12 months
key_facts.basis: Not seasonally adjusted; the smallest 12-month increase since March 2021, per the release

key_facts.label: Gasoline
key_facts.basis: Monthly seasonally adjusted and unadjusted changes, as reported

key_facts.label: Shelter
key_facts.basis: 12-month rise the smallest since November 2021; lodging away from home −3.5%

key_facts.label: Core goods
key_facts.basis: Commodities less food and energy commodities, Table A

channels.title: Disinflation and the policy path (shorter maturities)
channels.source_fact: Headline −0.1 percent and core +0.1 percent on the month; core 2.8 percent over 12 months, the smallest since March 2021.
channels.interpretation: Soft monthly readings support the case that inflation is moving toward target, which would tend to bring expected cuts forward and lower shorter yields, if investors took the month at face value. Without a sourced expectation, the case cannot say whether the softness was news.

channels.title: Energy and inflation compensation (longer maturities)
channels.source_fact: Energy −2.4 percent and seasonally adjusted gasoline −6.3 percent on the month; energy −3.3 percent over 12 months.
channels.interpretation: Lower energy prices reduce near-term inflation and could trim inflation compensation in longer yields. Energy is volatile and investors usually look through it, so this channel is weak for longer maturities.

channels.title: Volatile services (all maturities)
channels.source_fact: Airline fares −5.3 percent, lodging away from home −3.5 percent; motor vehicle insurance also fell.
channels.interpretation: Part of the core softness came from volatile services. A reader who discounts them would see a smaller decline in underlying inflation, which weakens the first channel.

competing_explanations.title: Seasonal adjustment flips the sign
competing_explanations.detail: Before seasonal adjustment the all items index rose 0.2 percent; the monthly decline is a seasonally adjusted figure, driven largely by gasoline's seasonal pattern. A reader relying on unadjusted or 12-month figures would see less disinflation than the headline suggests.

competing_explanations.title: Rents still firm
competing_explanations.detail: Owners' equivalent rent rose 0.4 percent and rent 0.3 percent; the low shelter figure depended on lodging away from home, a volatile component. A reader focused on rents would see less progress than the shelter total implies.

competing_explanations.title: A reading that cannot see later changes
competing_explanations.detail: The release covers March prices. Price changes after March, including any from policy changes announced after the reference month, cannot appear in it, so a soft March says little about the months that follow.

assumptions: Investors read core and services excluding energy as signals of the trend, and energy as largely transitory.
A soft month is read against the 12-month trend, not on its own.
Policy at the time was sensitive at the margin to inflation news.
missing_information: A sourced, contemporaneous consensus for headline and core CPI. Without it this case cannot say whether the release was a surprise.
Unrounded monthly changes; a 0.1 percent core reading could round from anywhere between 0.05 and 0.15 percent.
Import price data or import shares by category, to judge how later trade-cost changes might pass through.
The personal consumption expenditures price index for March, the Federal Reserve's target measure, published later; not used.
weakening_observations: If the next month showed a rebound in core services, March's softness would look like noise.
If the seasonal factors updated in February 2026 materially changed March's adjusted figures, the monthly decline could change; this case does not check the revised values.
If a sourced consensus had expected similar figures, the policy-path channel would be close to inactive for this release.

critique.title: A seasonally adjusted fall inside an unadjusted rise
critique.detail: 'Prices fell' is true only after seasonal adjustment; before adjustment the index rose 0.2 percent. The case reports both, but an analysis that leads with the adjusted decline risks overstating how much prices actually eased in March.

critique.title: Volatile components carry the month
critique.detail: Gasoline, airline fares and hotel prices account for much of the softness. The case names them but cannot separate trend from volatility without a longer history than one release provides.

critique.title: Timing limits the reading
critique.detail: This is a March reading published in April. Anything that changed prices after March is absent, and extrapolating March forward would misread what the release can show.

critique.title: First of four, read later
critique.detail: The first of four consecutive CPI releases in the library, included by that rule and analysed in October 2026 by an AI assistant that may know how inflation evolved afterwards. The text stays with the release, but hindsight may still shape its emphasis.

source_notes.title: Text used
source_notes.detail: The archived release as published, which shows 'Last Modified Date: April 10, 2025'. Figures come from the release text and Table A.

source_notes.title: Seasonal-factor revisions
source_notes.detail: BLS updates CPI seasonal factors each February and revises the previous five years of seasonally adjusted data, as its June 2025 release states. The monthly changes here are as first published; later revised values are not checked.

source_notes.title: Methodology note in the release
source_notes.detail: The release announced that, from the April data, BLS would replace survey data for the leased cars and trucks index with vendor transaction data. It does not affect the March figures used here.

provenance.method: Read the archived March 2025 CPI release on 2026-10-05, and the archived June 2025 CPI release for its statement of the seasonal-revision schedule. Facts come from the release text and Table A; the channels, competing explanations and critique are the assistant's interpretation. No market prices, forecasts, surveys or news coverage were used.
